extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of comparative politics, constitutional law, and history
extracted.subtask_description: Explanatory appendix material from a 19th-century comparative study of American and European institutions, summarizing rules and customary practices (inheritance, voting, juries, impeachment, press regulation, parliamentary power, etc.). Useful for learners of constitutional design and historical legal practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: American intestate succession rule
rubrics_metrics.description: If a man dies intestate, his property goes to his heirs in a direct line. If he has but one heir or heiress, he or she succeeds to the whole. If there are several heirs of the same degree, they divide the inheritance equally amongst them, without distinction of sex.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This rule was first prescribed in New York by a statute of February 23, 1786 and has since been adopted in other states. Exception: Vermont (male heir inherits a double portion). The American law also gives the testator broad freedom to dispose of property by will (e.g., New York: 'entire liberty, power, and authority, to dispose of his property by will... provided he do not leave it to a political body or any corporation').

rubrics_metrics.name: Status and abolition/modification of entails (fee tail)
rubrics_metrics.description: Estates tail were abolished in various American states at different times (e.g., Virginia in 1776, New York in 1786) and have been suppressed or modified by legislation in many others.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Some states never introduced entail (Vermont, Indiana, Illinois, South Carolina, Louisiana). Where preserved, it was often modified to reduce aristocratic tendencies. The general American principle favors the free circulation of property.

rubrics_metrics.name: French inheritance law (forced distribution)
rubrics_metrics.description: The French law obliges the testator to divide his property equally, or nearly so, among his heirs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Contrast with American practice: in France the testator's freedom is much more constrained, which the author characterizes as 'infinitely more democratic' in terms of inheritance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Voter qualifications (age, residence, property/tax/military service)
rubrics_metrics.description: All the States agree in granting the right of voting at the age of twenty-one. In all of them it is necessary to have resided for a certain time in the district where the vote is given (varies from three months to two years). Property/income, tax-paying, or militia-service qualifications vary by state.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: State-specific examples given: Massachusetts — income of Pound 3 or capital of Pound 60; Rhode Island — landed property of $133; Connecticut — property giving income of $17 or a year of militia service; New Jersey — property of Pound 50 a year; South Carolina and Maryland — fifty acres of land; many states (Mississippi, Ohio, Georgia, Virginia, Pennsylvania, Delaware, New York) require payment of taxes only; Maine and New Hampshire allow any man not on the pauper list to vote; several states have no property reference (Missouri, Alabama, Illinois, Louisiana, Indiana, Kentucky, Vermont). North Carolina applies different conditions for Senate vs House elections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Municipal self-government vs centralization
rubrics_metrics.description: Every corporation and every community of citizens retained the right of administering its own affairs; this right is described as part of the primitive constitution and 'the right of nature, and of reason.' Centralization deprives communities of this right through administrative controls (example: Intendant's authorization making local deliberations null).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quoted criticism (Malesherbes): central power prevents convocation of national assemblies, annuls community deliberations unless authorized, controls undertakings, employs favored workmen, etc. Historical observation: centralization in France pre-dates and was perfected by the Revolution and later regimes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Immutability of certain constitutional provisions (French context)
rubrics_metrics.description: A part of the French constitution is immutable (e.g., order of succession to the throne founded on natural succession), and some laws (1814, 1830 charters) leave no ordinary legislative means to change the constitution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argument: Because King, Peers, and Deputies derive authority from the constitution, they cannot legally change the charter without destroying their own legal basis; thus the charter appears effectively unchangeable by ordinary means. Contrast with England (no written constitution), where changes are less identifiable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Parliamentary sovereignty (England)
rubrics_metrics.description: It is a fundamental principle with English lawyers that Parliament can do everything except making a woman a man, or a man a woman; Parliament has sovereign and uncontrollable authority in making, confirming, enlarging, restraining, abrogating, repealing, reviving, and expounding of laws of all possible denominations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Blackstone's exposition: Parliament can alter succession, change established religion, create or change the constitution (Act of Union, triennial/septennial elections). Described as 'omnipotence of Parliament' in practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Political jurisdiction, impeachment, and punishments
rubrics_metrics.description: Most American constitutions give the exclusive right of impeachment to the House of Delegates (except North Carolina). Almost all constitutions give the exclusive right of pronouncing sentence to the Senate (or equivalent). The usual punishments political tribunals can inflict are removal or interdiction of public functions; only Virginia empowered other punishments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Crimes subject to political jurisdiction enumerated differently by state: federal constitution and some states list high treason, bribery, and other high crimes/offences; other states include misconduct, maladministration, corruption, intrigue; several states specify no particular offences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Press regulation and colonial censorship practice
rubrics_metrics.description: Attempts at preliminary security and censorship existed in the American colonies: e.g., a Massachusetts 1722 committee found a journal's 'tendency... to turn religion into derision' and recommended forbidding the printer from publishing without prior submission to the Secretary and requiring bail.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although such laws were enacted, enforcement could be evaded (example: the journal used Benjamin Franklin's name to elude prohibition), and public opinion sometimes resisted censorship. Grounds for suppression included insulting the government, disturbing peace, and irreligious or profane treatment of sacred writers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Jury formation and eligibility in the United States
rubrics_metrics.description: Federal courts select jurors from ordinary jury lists that each State prepares. In America, all citizens who exercise the elective franchise have the right of serving upon a jury (with some state-specific differences). Local magistrates (selectmen, supervisors, trustees, sheriffs) choose a county list of eligible jurors; jurors for a trial are drawn by lot from that list.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical features: lists are chosen annually by elective municipal or county magistrates, names transmitted to County Court, jurors receive indemnification (about a dollar per day plus travel expenses), jury service intended to be a broadly accessible civic duty and made as little onerous as possible. New York had fewer persons eligible as jurymen than electors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Role and limits of juries in civil proceedings (English practice)
rubrics_metrics.description: In civil cases in England, jurors are under the immediate control of the judge. The verdict of the jury in civil cases comprises both facts and legal right, but the judge may refuse to receive the verdict and a new trial may be awarded.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Contrast with criminal practice where jury infallibility is stronger. Reference: Blackstone's Commentaries (book iii, ch. 24).

rubrics_metrics.name: Equality, morals, and public order
rubrics_metrics.description: It is not the equality of conditions which makes men immoral and irreligious; but when men, being equal, are at the same time immoral and irreligious, the effects of immorality and irreligion easily manifest themselves outwardly, because men have but little influence upon each other, and no class exists which can undertake to keep society in order.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Equality itself does not engender profligacy, but it can allow existing immorality to be more visible and less checked by intermediary classes or institutions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public opinion as an imperfect indicator of legal excellence
rubrics_metrics.description: Setting aside those who do not think or dare not speak, the great majority of Americans appear satisfied with their political institutions; this is an indication but not a demonstration of the absolute excellence of American laws.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: One should not judge laws solely by popular attachment, because popular opinion changes with age and circumstance; historical examples (England, France) show that attachment does not guarantee correctness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Democratic pacification of the military as a political risk
rubrics_metrics.description: If the love of physical gratification and the taste for well-being, which are suggested by equality, were to possess the mind of a democratic people, the manners would become opposed to military tastes. Troops might prefer the comforts of a peace establishment, take up arms without enthusiasm, and use them without energy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consequences: an army pacified by democratic tastes might still engage in revolutions (which gratify ambition at less cost than war), but would be less effective in conventional military defense. This is presented as a rare but formidable peril to democratic nations.
